summary: Beyoncé's concert film "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" opened at number one with an estimated $21 million in North America, a strong result for a normally slow post-Thanksgiving weekend. It fell short of Taylor Swift's "The Eras Tour" debut but beat earlier concert film records, and both artists distributed through AMC Theatres. The article also covers the rest of the top 10, including "Godzilla Minus One," and the outlook for 2023 box office.
one_line: Beyoncé's "Renaissance" concert film debuted first at the box office with $21 million, the best early-December opening in 20 years.
key_facts: "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" opened in first place with $21 million in North American ticket sales, per AMC Theatres estimates on Sunday.
It is the first film to open over $20 million on the post-Thanksgiving weekend in 20 years, not adjusting for inflation (since "The Last Samurai").
The film debuted in 2,539 theaters in the U.S. and Canada and in 94 international territories, where it earned $6.4 million from 2,621 theaters.
Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour debuted to $92.8 million in October and is wrapping up its theatrical run with over $250 million globally.
Before Swift, the biggest concert film debuts (Miley Cyrus 2008 and Justin Bieber 2011) had not surpassed an unadjusted $32 million.
The 39-city, 56-show Renaissance tour began in Stockholm in May, ended in Kansas City, Missouri, made over $500 million and drew over 2.7 million concertgoers.
Both Beyoncé and Swift partnered with AMC Theatres rather than a traditional studio and are reported to receive at least 50% of ticket sales.
Renaissance tickets averaged around $23.32 versus $20.78 for Swift's film, per EntTelligence; the audience was around 900,000 and skewed a bit older.
Renaissance holds 100% on Rotten Tomatoes and an A+ CinemaScore.
"The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" was second with $14.5 million and over $121 million domestically.
"Godzilla Minus One" took third with $11 million from 2,308 locations, the biggest opening for a foreign film in the U.S. this year; it cost $15 million to produce and earned $23 million in Japan.
Disney's "Wish" fell 62% to $7.4 million, and "The Marvels" has a $197 million global tally against a reported $300 million cost.
Ridley Scott's "Napoleon" earned $7.1 million in its second weekend, $45.7 million domestically against a $200 million budget.
The top 10 films were expected to gross only $85 million total, and the industry is heading toward a $9 billion year versus the $11 billion pre-pandemic norm.
